title: Slack & PR Communication
theme: Natural Slack replies and soft disagreement
review: Acknowledge, question gently, and take ownership without sounding formal.

phrases.meaning: I’ll check or investigate it. Natural for reported bugs, review requests, or odd behavior.
phrases.use: Use when someone reports an issue or asks you to inspect something.
phrases.avoid: For a deeper investigation, “I’ll dig into it” may fit better.
phrases.example: “The mobile preview looks a bit off on Safari.” → “I’ll take a look.”
phrases.mistake: Avoid overly formal wording like “I will investigate this problem” in normal Slack conversation.
phrases.pronunciation: “take a” blends together, roughly “tay-kuh.”

phrases.meaning: It acknowledges the other person’s reasoning. It can mean something is reasonable without meaning full agreement.
phrases.use: Use in product or design discussion before adding your own thought.
phrases.avoid: Don’t use it mechanically after every message; it should signal real understanding.
phrases.example: “That makes sense. I’m just wondering if we can do it without another state.”
phrases.mistake: “Makes sense” is fine in Slack, but “That makes sense” sounds a little warmer.
phrases.pronunciation: The final t in “that” is often soft in fast speech.

phrases.text: I’m not sure we need to…
phrases.meaning: A soft way to question whether something is necessary.
phrases.use: Use to challenge extra complexity without rejecting the idea aggressively.
phrases.avoid: If something is objectively wrong, be clearer instead of softening it too much.
phrases.example: “I’m not sure we need to add another modal. Could we handle it inside the existing panel?”
phrases.mistake: Avoid blunt alternatives like “This is unnecessary” when you want collaboration.
phrases.pronunciation: “to” is usually reduced to “tuh.”

dialogue: I added another confirmation modal before users disconnect their custom UI.
That makes sense from a safety point of view, but I’m not sure we need to add another modal. We already have a confirmation step in the panel.
Fair point. Can you check whether we can reuse that one?
exercise: Reply to a reported mobile bug using “I’ll take a look.”
Respond to a design idea with “That makes sense” and add your own thought.
Question a new dependency with “I’m not sure we need to…”
mixedDialogue: The mobile editor is showing a second confirmation before users leave the page.
That makes sense if we are protecting unsaved work.
Do you think we should keep both confirmations?
I am not sure we need to. We already warn them when there are unsaved changes.
Can you check the existing flow?
Yep, I will take a look and reply in the thread.

title: Clarifying & Suggesting
theme: Clarifying requirements and stating preferences
review: Clarify first, suggest collaboratively, then state your preference.

phrases.text: Just to make sure I understand…
phrases.meaning: Confirms your interpretation before you code.
phrases.use: Use when a requirement has an important boundary or could be interpreted in multiple ways.
phrases.avoid: For a tiny factual question, a shorter direct question is usually better.
phrases.example: “Just to make sure I understand, the mobile view should still be fully editable, right?”
phrases.mistake: Avoid “I want to ensure that I have understood correctly” in casual team communication.
phrases.pronunciation: “just to” often becomes “jus-tuh.”

phrases.meaning: A collaborative way to suggest an option and invite feedback.
phrases.use: Use for product, UX, or implementation ideas that are still open.
phrases.avoid: Don’t use it for something that is already a confirmed requirement.
phrases.example: “What do you think about moving this button into the toolbar?”
phrases.mistake: “What do you think of…?” often asks for an opinion about an existing thing; “about + -ing” works well for actions.
phrases.pronunciation: Keep “what do you” light; the stress usually lands on the proposed idea.

phrases.meaning: Shows your current preference among several reasonable choices.
phrases.use: Use when you prefer one implementation but are open to discussion.
phrases.avoid: Not suitable when a requirement is objectively fixed.
phrases.example: “I’d lean toward reusing the existing component.”
phrases.mistake: Avoid turning it into a command; the point is to signal a preference, not certainty.
phrases.pronunciation: “I’d lean” flows together; stress “lean.”

dialogue: We could add a new modal or reuse the current panel.
Just to make sure I understand, we only need one confirmation step, right?
What do you think about reusing the existing panel? I’d lean toward that so we avoid another component.
exercise: Clarify a mobile editor requirement.
Suggest moving a control to an existing toolbar.
State a preference between two technical approaches.
mixedDialogue: I want the mobile toolbar to stay visible while users edit.
Just to make sure I understand, it should stay fixed while the canvas scrolls, right?
That makes sense. What do you think about reusing the existing desktop toolbar container?
I would lean toward that. I will take a look at the responsive behavior first.

title: Bugs & Uncertainty
theme: Debugging without overclaiming
review: State uncertainty, share the current hypothesis, then give a practical next step.

phrases.meaning: Current evidence suggests something, but you are not claiming absolute certainty.
phrases.use: Use while debugging or summarizing what you currently see.
phrases.avoid: If you already verified the cause, state it directly.
phrases.example: “It looks like the external styles aren’t loading in the embed.”
phrases.mistake: Don’t say “It is look like.” The correct form is “It looks like.”
phrases.pronunciation: The “s” in “looks” connects naturally into “like.”

phrases.text: I haven’t dug into it yet.
phrases.meaning: You know about the issue but have not investigated deeply yet.
phrases.use: Use to set expectations without sounding defensive.
phrases.avoid: Don’t use it after you already did a full investigation.
phrases.example: “I haven’t dug into it yet, but it looks like it might be related to the external styles.”
phrases.mistake: More natural than “I didn’t investigate it yet” in casual engineering conversation.
phrases.pronunciation: “dug into” often flows like “dug-in-tuh.”

phrases.meaning: Introduces a pragmatic temporary recommendation.
phrases.use: Use when you want to move forward without pretending the decision is permanent.
phrases.avoid: Don’t use it for a final architecture decision that has already been confirmed.
phrases.example: “For now, I’d keep the existing component and fix the mobile layout there.”
phrases.mistake: Avoid sounding vague; say exactly what you would do next.
phrases.pronunciation: “for now” is often reduced slightly to “fer-now.”

dialogue: The embed is broken on Safari.
I haven’t dug into it yet, but it looks like the styles may not be loading.
Should we rewrite the embed component?
For now, I’d verify the stylesheet request first before changing the component.
exercise: Report a bug you have not fully investigated.
Give a current hypothesis.
Suggest a safe temporary next step.
mixedDialogue: The published form sometimes loses styling after refresh.
I have not dug into it yet, but it looks like the stylesheet request may be racing with the embed render.
For now, I would verify the request timing first. I am not sure we need to replace the loader yet.
Just to make sure I understand, this only happens in the published embed, not preview, right?

title: Polite PR Feedback
theme: Giving code-review feedback without sounding harsh
review: Ask for reasoning, then suggest simplification.

phrases.text: Could we simplify this a bit?
phrases.meaning: Questions unnecessary complexity in a collaborative way.
phrases.use: Use when you think the same result can be achieved with less code or fewer abstractions.
phrases.avoid: If the code is actually incorrect, explain the bug directly too.
phrases.example: “Could we simplify this a bit and keep the mobile logic inside the existing component?”
phrases.mistake: Softer and more useful than “This is too complicated.”
phrases.pronunciation: “Could we” often blends to “could-we.”

phrases.meaning: Asks for context before challenging a decision.
phrases.use: Use when code looks unusual and there may be hidden context.
phrases.avoid: Don’t use it sarcastically; keep the tone genuinely curious.
phrases.example: “What’s the reason for fetching this again instead of using the existing data?”
phrases.mistake: Often softer than “Why did you do this?”
phrases.pronunciation: “What’s the” flows quickly; stress the thing you’re asking about.

phrases.meaning: A soft recommendation to preserve the current or simpler approach.
phrases.use: Use when you have a preference but don’t need to turn it into a hard rule.
phrases.avoid: Don’t use it for a requirement that must be followed exactly.
phrases.example: “I’d probably keep this in the existing component instead of creating another one.”
phrases.mistake: “probably” is useful because it signals recommendation rather than command.
phrases.pronunciation: Stress “keep”; “probably” is often reduced in fast speech.

dialogue: I split this into a new hook and two components.
What’s the reason for keeping this state separate?
Mostly to make the file smaller.
Got it. Could we simplify this a bit? I’d probably keep the state in the existing component until we actually reuse it.
exercise: Question one abstraction in a PR.
Ask for reasoning behind a second fetch.
Suggest keeping logic in the current component.
mixedDialogue: I added a new hook just for the mobile breakpoint state.
What is the reason for keeping that state separate from the existing editor state?
I might be missing something, but could we simplify this a bit and keep one source of truth?
I would probably keep it in the editor state for now, then revisit it if we actually reuse the hook.

title: Standups & Blockers
theme: Concise progress updates
review: Progress → issue → blocker → next step.

phrases.meaning: You’re in the final stage of a task.
phrases.use: Use when a task is nearly complete.
phrases.avoid: Don’t use it when you just started.
phrases.example: “I’m wrapping up the sticky header fix today.”
phrases.mistake: “I’m working on…” can mean any stage; “wrapping up” specifically means nearly finished.
phrases.pronunciation: “wrapping up” links smoothly; stress “wrap.”

phrases.meaning: You cannot meaningfully continue because of a dependency.
phrases.use: Use for a real blocker such as an API, design decision, or unavailable environment.
phrases.avoid: For a small inconvenience with a workaround, say “I ran into an issue with…” instead.
phrases.example: “I’m blocked on the backend response format.”
phrases.mistake: Focus on the dependency, not blame: “blocked on the API contract,” not “blocked by X person.”
phrases.pronunciation: “blocked on” sounds like “blockt-on.”

phrases.meaning: You encountered an unexpected problem.
phrases.use: Use in standups or Slack when something interrupted progress.
phrases.avoid: It does not automatically mean you’re blocked.
phrases.example: “I ran into an issue with sticky headers in the virtualized table.”
phrases.mistake: Much more natural than “I faced a problem.”
phrases.pronunciation: “ran into” flows together: “ran-in-tuh.”

dialogue: I’m wrapping up the sticky header fix. I ran into an overflow issue yesterday, but that part is fixed now.
I’m blocked on the final API response shape for the last state.
exercise: Write one standup sentence with “wrapping up.”
Describe a problem you encountered with “ran into.”
Describe a real dependency with “blocked on.”
mixedDialogue: How is the sticky table header task going?
I am wrapping up the main fix. I ran into an overflow issue in the virtualized container, but that part is resolved.
I am blocked on the final empty-state behavior. Just to make sure I understand, should the header stay visible when there are zero rows?
Great. I will finish that path once the API response is confirmed.

title: Technical Trade-offs
theme: Explaining engineering decisions clearly
review: Trade-off → downside → whether the benefit is worth it.

phrases.meaning: Explains what you gain and what you give up.
phrases.use: Use when comparing two technically valid options.
phrases.avoid: Don’t use it if there is no real trade-off and one option is simply broken.
phrases.example: “The trade-off is that this approach is simpler, but it gives us less flexibility later.”
phrases.mistake: More natural in engineering discussion than a long “advantages and disadvantages” framing.
phrases.pronunciation: Stress “trade-off.”

phrases.meaning: Names the biggest negative consequence of an approach.
phrases.use: Use when you want to keep the discussion balanced.
phrases.avoid: If there are several equal risks, say “There are a few downsides.”
phrases.example: “The main downside is duplicated logic.”
phrases.mistake: Softer and more analytical than “This is bad because…”
phrases.pronunciation: Stress “main” and “downside.”

phrases.meaning: The benefit justifies the cost, complexity, or effort.
phrases.use: Use after you’ve explained the cost honestly.
phrases.avoid: If you’re still unsure, say “I’m not sure it’s worth it.”
phrases.example: “It adds a little more code, but I think it’s worth it for the better mobile UX.”
phrases.mistake: Don’t say “it worth it”; you need “it’s worth it.”
phrases.pronunciation: “it’s worth it” links together quickly.

dialogue: This adds a shared hook and a little more state.
The trade-off is that we add some complexity now, but both editor views stay in sync.
The main downside is more state coordination, but I think it’s worth it for consistent behavior.
exercise: Explain one real technical trade-off.
Name its main downside.
Say whether you think the cost is worth it.
mixedDialogue: We can either duplicate the mobile layout or share the same component.
The trade-off is that sharing it adds a little branching, but it keeps behavior consistent.
The main downside is more conditional styling in one component.
Yes, I think it is worth it. I would probably keep one component unless the mobile flow starts diverging a lot.

title: Polite Pushback
theme: Disagreeing without friction
review: Acknowledge → raise concern → state preference.

phrases.text: I see where you’re coming from.
phrases.meaning: Shows that you understand the reasoning even if you don’t fully agree.
phrases.use: Use before pushback in product or technical discussion.
phrases.avoid: Not useful for a purely factual statement.
phrases.example: “I see where you’re coming from. I’m just worried we’ll maintain the same logic in two places.”
phrases.mistake: Use it only when you genuinely understand the other side.
phrases.pronunciation: “where you’re” often blends naturally.

phrases.meaning: Signals that you’re mostly okay with the idea but have one important worry.
phrases.use: Use when there is one main risk to discuss.
phrases.avoid: If you have several concerns, say “I have a few concerns.”
phrases.example: “My only concern is that users might think the template is permanently connected to that form.”
phrases.mistake: Avoid stacking multiple unrelated concerns after saying “only.”
phrases.pronunciation: Stress “only concern.”

phrases.meaning: States a clear preference, stronger than “I’d lean toward.”
phrases.use: Use when you want to be direct about your preferred path.
phrases.avoid: Avoid if you don’t actually have a strong preference.
phrases.example: “I’d rather fix the root issue than add another workaround.”
phrases.mistake: Correct: “I’d rather keep…” not “I’d rather to keep…”
phrases.pronunciation: “I’d rather” is smooth; stress the verb that follows.

dialogue: Could we just add a second setting for this?
I see where you’re coming from. My only concern is that we’ll create two sources of truth.
I’d rather reuse the existing form context and keep one place responsible for it.
exercise: Acknowledge an approach you disagree with.
Raise one concern.
State what you’d rather do instead.
mixedDialogue: Could we add another config flag for this behavior?
I see where you are coming from. My only concern is that we would create a second source of truth.
I would rather derive it from the existing form context. The trade-off is a little more logic in one place, but I think it is worth it.
Could we simplify the config and keep the behavior derived instead?

title: Confidence & Uncertainty
theme: Sounding confident without overclaiming
review: Current understanding → room for missing context → promise an update.

phrases.meaning: Based on the information you currently have, something appears true.
phrases.use: Use when you have evidence but haven’t proven every detail.
phrases.avoid: If something is fully verified, state it directly.
phrases.example: “From what I can tell, this only happens in the mobile editor.”
phrases.mistake: Avoid translated wording like “As I can understand…”
phrases.pronunciation: “what I” blends together in normal speech.

phrases.text: I might be missing something, but…
phrases.meaning: You think there may be a problem, while leaving room for missing context.
phrases.use: Excellent in PR reviews and architecture discussions.
phrases.avoid: Don’t overuse it when the bug is factual and confirmed.
phrases.example: “I might be missing something, but do we need to fetch this data again here?”
phrases.mistake: The phrase should soften uncertainty, not hide a clear bug.
phrases.pronunciation: Stress “missing” lightly; the rest flows quickly.

phrases.meaning: You’ll update the other person when you know more or something changes.
phrases.use: Use when investigation or progress will continue.
phrases.avoid: Don’t use it if you don’t actually intend to send an update.
phrases.example: “I’m checking the Safari issue now. I’ll keep you posted.”
phrases.mistake: More natural than “I will inform you about the progress.”
phrases.pronunciation: “keep you” often sounds like “keep-yuh.”

dialogue: Do we need backend changes for this?
From what I can tell, no. I might be missing something, but the API already returns everything the editor needs.
Yep, I’ll test the full flow and keep you posted.
exercise: State a careful technical conclusion.
Question a possible redundant fetch.
Promise an update on an investigation.
mixedDialogue: Do we need a backend change for answer piping?
From what I can tell, no. I might be missing something, but the current endpoint already returns the fields we need.
It looks like they are already in the contract. My only concern is how we handle duplicates.
Yep. I will test the full flow and keep you posted.

title: Scoping & Proposing Changes
theme: Keeping v1 focused
review: Limit scope, keep decisions reversible, and define what is enough for now.

phrases.meaning: I think we should limit this change to a specific area for now.
phrases.use: Use when a task is starting to grow beyond its original goal.
phrases.avoid: If the wider scope is explicitly required, don’t artificially narrow it.
phrases.example: “I’d keep this scoped to the template editor for now.”
phrases.mistake: Better than “Don’t change anything else.”
phrases.pronunciation: “scoped to” often blends like “scoped-tuh.”

phrases.text: We can always revisit this later.
phrases.meaning: We don’t need to solve everything now; we can come back to it if needed.
phrases.use: Use to avoid premature complexity and keep decisions reversible.
phrases.avoid: Don’t defer critical security, correctness, or data-loss issues.
phrases.example: “Let’s ship the simpler version first. We can always revisit this later.”
phrases.mistake: It does not mean “never”; it means “not necessary now.”
phrases.pronunciation: Stress “revisit” and “later.”

phrases.text: That should be enough for now.
phrases.meaning: The current solution is sufficient at this stage.
phrases.use: Use when the v1 behavior covers the main requirement.
phrases.avoid: By itself, “that should be enough” can sound dismissive; “for now” softens it.
phrases.example: “If we pass the form slug into the editor and preselect it, that should be enough for now.”
phrases.mistake: Avoid formal wording like “This solution is sufficient for the current phase.”
phrases.pronunciation: “should be” and “for now” are both often lightly reduced.

dialogue: Should we let templates connect to multiple forms at the same time?
I’d keep this scoped to one active form context for now.
What if users need fields from several forms?
We can always revisit this later if that becomes common. Switching the active form should cover the main need.
Yeah, I think that should be enough for now.
exercise: Limit one feature to v1 scope.
Defer one non-critical idea.
Describe what is sufficient for the first version.
mixedDialogue: Should v1 support templates connected to multiple forms at once?
I would keep this scoped to one active form context for now.
Are we limiting ourselves too much?
From what I can tell, one context covers the current use cases. The main downside of multi-form support is much more state coordination.
We can always revisit this later. That should be enough for now.

title: Aligning on Requirements
theme: Confirming shared understanding before coding
review: State your interpretation → confirm the important boundary → check alignment.

phrases.text: Just to make sure we’re on the same page…
phrases.meaning: Confirms that you and the other person understand the requirement in the same way.
phrases.use: Use after meetings or before implementing an ambiguous requirement.
phrases.avoid: For one tiny factual question, use a shorter direct question.
phrases.example: “Just to make sure we’re on the same page, the form context is only for field lookup and isn’t saved on the template, right?”
phrases.mistake: More natural than “To be sure we have the same idea…”
phrases.pronunciation: “Just to” becomes “jus-tuh”; keep the phrase light and conversational.

phrases.meaning: This is how I currently interpret the requirement; correct me if I’m wrong.
phrases.use: Use to summarize your interpretation before implementation.
phrases.avoid: If you’ve already confirmed the fact, state it directly.
phrases.example: “My understanding is that we only need the three visibility toggles and should keep the rest of block.config untouched.”
phrases.mistake: Not “My understand is that…” — you need the noun “understanding.”
phrases.pronunciation: Stress “STAND” in “understanding.”

phrases.text: Does that line up with what you had in mind?
phrases.meaning: Does my proposed solution match what you were imagining?
phrases.use: Use after translating product or design intent into an implementation plan.
phrases.avoid: For hard factual checks, use “Is that correct?” instead.
phrases.example: “I’ll keep it frontend-only and reuse the existing header component. Does that line up with what you had in mind?”
phrases.mistake: Avoid “Is it match with your idea?”
phrases.pronunciation: “Does that” and “what you” blend naturally in normal speech.

dialogue: For table headers, I want users to hide Search, New row, and the title.
My understanding is that we’re only adding visibility settings for those three controls and keeping the rest of the current config unchanged.
Just to make sure we’re on the same page, these settings live in block.config and should work in editor, preview, and published app.
Great. I’ll keep it frontend-only and reuse the existing header component. Does that line up with what you had in mind?
exercise: Write a Slack reply confirming an editor requirement.
State your understanding of what should not be persisted.
Finish by checking whether your approach matches the PM’s intent.
mixedDialogue: For the table block, users should be able to hide Search, New row, and the title.
My understanding is that those are the only new visibility settings.
Just to make sure we are on the same page, they live in block.config and work in editor, preview, and published app.
I would keep this scoped to those three controls. Does that line up with what you had in mind?

title: Root Cause & Debugging Updates
theme: Explaining what you discovered after debugging
review: Discovery → root cause → symptom explained.

phrases.meaning: I investigated it, and the actual situation is different from what we first thought.
phrases.use: Use after you have verified a debugging discovery.
phrases.avoid: If you are still guessing, use “From what I can tell…” instead.
phrases.example: “It turns out the API response is fine. We were resetting the local state after the contract reload.”
phrases.mistake: More natural than “Finally I understood that the problem is…”
phrases.pronunciation: “it turns out” links together; stress “turns” and “out.”

phrases.meaning: There are several details, but the core problem is this.
phrases.use: Use to explain a technical root cause clearly.
phrases.avoid: Don’t oversimplify if there are several unrelated causes.
phrases.example: “The issue comes down to scroll ownership.”
phrases.mistake: If you say “related,” use “related to,” not “related with.”
phrases.pronunciation: “comes down to” sounds like “cumz-down-tuh.”

phrases.meaning: Now the symptom makes sense because we found the reason.
phrases.use: Use to connect a discovered cause to visible behavior.
phrases.avoid: If the cause is only possible, say “That could explain why…”
phrases.example: “We rebuild answers from defaults every time the tab becomes visible. That explains why users lose what they typed.”
phrases.mistake: Not “This explains me why…” — say “This explains why…”
phrases.pronunciation: Stress “PLAINS” in “explains.”

dialogue: On tab refocus, refreshContract uses preserveInProgressAnswers=false.
Ah, that explains why the fields are clearing when users come back to the tab.
I thought the fetch itself was the problem.
Same. It turns out the fetch is fine. The issue comes down to how we rebuild derived state after the refresh.
exercise: Describe a debugging discovery with “It turns out…”.
Explain a root cause with “The issue comes down to…”.
Connect that cause to a symptom with “That explains why…”.
mixedDialogue: I found why answers disappear after tab refocus.
We rebuild derived state with preserveInProgressAnswers set to false.
That explains why the fields reset. It turns out the fetch itself is fine.
So the issue is local state?
Exactly. The issue comes down to how we rebuild it. From what I can tell, we can fix that without touching the API.

title: Suggesting a Direction
theme: Proposing a technical direction without sounding forceful
review: Perspective → suggestion → expected result.

phrases.meaning: I think this may be a good direction — what do you think?
phrases.use: Use for technical or product proposals that are still open to discussion.
phrases.avoid: For a confirmed bug or hard requirement, be more direct.
phrases.example: “Would it make sense to reuse the existing table header component here?”
phrases.mistake: Not “Is it make sense to…?”
phrases.pronunciation: “Would it” blends naturally; “to” is often reduced.

phrases.meaning: Based on the design, this is the behavior I think should happen.
phrases.use: Useful when reasoning about expected behavior you haven’t fully verified.
phrases.avoid: If you tested it already, state the result directly.
phrases.example: “Once the table owns the scroll, I’d expect the existing sticky-cell logic to work.”
phrases.mistake: Prefer “I’d expect this to work” over “I expect that it should be working.”
phrases.pronunciation: “I’d expect” flows like “eye-dik-SPEKT.”

phrases.meaning: This is how I currently understand the situation or trade-off.
phrases.use: Use when there are multiple valid directions and you want to explain your reasoning.
phrases.avoid: Not for objective facts you already know.
phrases.example: “The way I see it, the form context is only needed while editing, so I wouldn’t persist it on the template.”
phrases.mistake: More natural than “In my view point…”
phrases.pronunciation: “The way I” connects smoothly; keep it light.

dialogue: Should we add another config value so the table knows whether it owns the page scroll?
The way I see it, the table should already own the scroll everywhere we need sticky headers.
So you’d rather fix the layout chain?
Yeah. Would it make sense to fix the container height and min-height chain first?
Exactly. Once the table is the scroll owner, I’d expect the existing sticky logic to work without another setting.
exercise: Suggest a smaller implementation.
Describe expected component behavior after a fix.
Explain why you prefer a frontend-only approach.
mixedDialogue: Should we add another config value to control sticky headers?
The way I see it, the table should already own the scroll in the layouts where sticky headers are supported.
Would it make sense to fix the height and min-height chain first?
Once the table owns the scroll, I would expect the existing sticky logic to work. Does that line up with what you had in mind?

title: Reporting Blockers Clearly
theme: Communicating dependencies without blame
review: Blocked = cannot continue; waiting on = dependency exists; pick back up = when you will resume.

phrases.meaning: You genuinely can’t make meaningful progress until something else happens.
phrases.use: Use for real blockers in standups.
phrases.avoid: If you can keep working elsewhere, “waiting on” may be more accurate.
phrases.example: “I’m blocked on the backend response shape for the new row-count condition.”
phrases.mistake: Focus on the dependency, not the person.
phrases.pronunciation: “blocked on” sounds like “blockt-on.”

phrases.meaning: You need something from another person, team, deployment, or process, but you may still have other work.
phrases.use: Use for dependencies that are not fully blocking you.
phrases.avoid: Don’t overstate it as a blocker if you still have meaningful work available.
phrases.example: “I’m waiting on the staging deploy to verify the submit flow.”
phrases.mistake: “Waiting for” is also correct; “waiting on” is especially common in workplace English.
phrases.pronunciation: “waiting on” flows together naturally.

phrases.text: I’ll pick this back up once…
phrases.meaning: I’m pausing this task now and will resume when a specific condition is met.
phrases.use: Use when you switch to another task instead of sitting idle.
phrases.avoid: Avoid vague “later”; name the condition.
phrases.example: “I’ll pick this back up once the API is on staging.”
phrases.mistake: More natural than “I will continue it again when backend is ready.”
phrases.pronunciation: “pick-this-back-up” is one rhythm, with stress on “back.”

dialogue: How’s the mobile editor toggle going?
The shell is done, but I’m blocked on the final mobile breakpoint because it affects the canvas width.
Perfect. I’m waiting on that decision, but I can still finish the toolbar states. I’ll pick the canvas work back up once the breakpoint is confirmed.
exercise: Write one true blocker.
Write one dependency that doesn’t stop all work.
Say exactly when you’ll resume a paused task.
mixedDialogue: Can you finish the mobile canvas today?
I am blocked on the final breakpoint decision, so I cannot finish the sizing yet.
Design should confirm it this afternoon.
Perfect. I am waiting on that, but I can finish the toolbar states meanwhile.
I will pick this back up once the breakpoint is confirmed, and I will keep you posted if anything else comes up.

title: Raising Edge Cases & Risks
theme: Surfacing risks without sounding negative
review: Possible risk → edge-case question → severity of feedback.

phrases.text: One thing to watch out for is…
phrases.meaning: There is a specific risk or edge case we should keep in mind.
phrases.use: Useful in PR reviews when something could become a problem.
phrases.avoid: If you already confirmed a real bug, say it directly.
phrases.example: “One thing to watch out for is resetting the user’s answers when the contract reloads.”
phrases.mistake: Avoid awkward “be careful about is about…” phrasing.
phrases.pronunciation: “watch out for” flows like “watch-out-fer.”

phrases.meaning: A neutral way to raise an edge case and reason together.
phrases.use: Use for realistic edge cases involving state, APIs, or product behavior.
phrases.avoid: Don’t generate endless hypothetical scenarios with little value.
phrases.example: “What happens if the form owner removes every field while the user has the page open?”
phrases.mistake: For product behavior, “What happens if…?” is often more natural than “What will happen if…?”
phrases.pronunciation: “what happens if” flows quickly.

phrases.text: I don’t think this is a blocker, but…
phrases.meaning: This is worth mentioning, but it should not stop the PR or release.
phrases.use: Use to label review severity clearly.
phrases.avoid: Not for correctness, security, data-loss, or core UX problems.
phrases.example: “I don’t think this is a blocker, but we should probably add a contract-reload test in a follow-up.”
phrases.mistake: More natural than “This is not blocking from my side.”
phrases.pronunciation: Stress “blocker.”

dialogue: I changed the mobile editor to use the same breakpoint constant as the public form.
Nice. One thing to watch out for is whether changing that constant affects existing preview behavior.
What happens if we change the public breakpoint later? Will the editor automatically stay in sync?
Perfect. I don’t think this is a blocker, but a small test around that shared breakpoint would make it safer.
exercise: Raise one risk in a PR.
Ask one meaningful edge-case question.
Give one non-blocking improvement comment.
mixedDialogue: I changed the editor and published form to use the same mobile breakpoint constant.
One thing to watch out for is whether changing that constant later affects both surfaces in the same way.
What happens if product wants a different editor preview width later?
Then we would need to split them.
That makes sense. I do not think this is a blocker, but would it make sense to add a small test around the shared behavior?

title: Checking Assumptions Early
theme: Avoiding unnecessary rework
review: Confirm the assumption early → invite hidden context → ask for a quick second opinion.

phrases.meaning: My current understanding points to one conclusion, but I want to check whether there is context I don’t know.
phrases.use: Use when code or a requirement looks unnecessary or inconsistent.
phrases.avoid: By itself it can sound sharp; give your reasoning first.
phrases.example: “We already fetch the form when the editor opens. Am I missing something, or do we not need a second fetch here?”
phrases.mistake: More natural than “Maybe I don’t understand something?”
phrases.pronunciation: “Am I” connects naturally; use a genuinely curious tone.

phrases.text: Before I go too far down this path…
phrases.meaning: I’ve started in one direction, but I want to confirm it before investing too much time.
phrases.use: Use early when one unclear decision could create rework.
phrases.avoid: Don’t say “Before I waste more time…” — it sounds negative.
phrases.example: “Before I go too far down this path, are we sure the mobile editor should share the exact same breakpoint?”
phrases.mistake: A useful shorter variant is “Before I go too far with this…”
phrases.pronunciation: “go too far” often sounds like “go-tuh-FAR.”

phrases.meaning: Can you quickly check whether my reasoning or approach makes sense?
phrases.use: Use for a quick second opinion, not a full review.
phrases.avoid: If you need a full code review, ask someone to “take a look at the PR.”
phrases.example: “Can you sanity-check my understanding of the submit flow? We compute formulas first, run submit logic second, then build the payload.”
phrases.mistake: More natural in engineering teams than “Can you check if my thinking is correct?”
phrases.pronunciation: “sanity” is “SAN-uh-tee,” stress on SAN.

dialogue: I’m looking at the answer-piping editor flow. The selected form seems to be needed only for field lookup, so I’m keeping it in local editor state.
Before I go too far down this path, I want to make sure there isn’t another place that expects the template to remember the form.
Perfect. I also don’t see any reason to add a second persisted config value here. Am I missing something?
Great. Can you sanity-check the PR once I’ve wired the formSlug entry point? Mainly the state flow, not the styling.
exercise: Ask an early clarification that could prevent rework.
Question one possibly unnecessary API call or state value.
Ask for a quick sanity-check of your technical reasoning.
mixedDialogue: Before I go too far down this path, I want to confirm the selected form is only editor context and should not be saved on the template.
Great. From what I can tell, local editor state is enough. Am I missing something?
No, that is the intended flow.
Can you sanity-check this before I open the PR? My only concern is whether another entry point expects persisted form context.
Sure. I will check the entry points.

title: Following Up Naturally
theme: Following up on work without sounding pushy
review: Spaced review: use ‘I’ll keep you posted’ when you owe someone an update, ‘I’m waiting on…’ for a dependency, and ‘Does that line up with what you had in mind?’ when you want to confirm alignment. Today we’ll focus on the other side of that conversation: checking back in with teammates naturally.

phrases.meaning: A friendly, low-pressure way to follow up on something you’re waiting for. It sounds much softer than demanding an update.
phrases.use: Use in Slack when you need a status update, decision, review, design, API change, or answer from a teammate.
phrases.avoid: Don’t use it repeatedly in a short period or when the other person has already given you a clear timeline. In urgent cases, be direct about the deadline instead.
phrases.example: Just checking in on the mobile breakpoint decision — do we have a final value now?
phrases.mistake: Avoid ‘I am following you up about…’. Natural options are ‘Just checking in on…’ or ‘Following up on…’.
phrases.pronunciation: ‘checking in on’ connects smoothly: CHECK-ing-in-on. Keep ‘just’ light so the phrase sounds casual rather than demanding.

phrases.meaning: A short, direct way to ask whether anything has changed since the last conversation. Neutral and very common in work chat.
phrases.use: Use when the context is already known and you mainly need the latest status.
phrases.avoid: It can feel abrupt if there has been no previous conversation or if the topic is sensitive. Add context or use ‘Just checking in on…’ when you want to sound warmer.
phrases.example: Any update on the staging deploy? I’d like to verify the submit flow once it’s up.
phrases.mistake: Avoid ‘Do you have any updates about this?’ when a short Slack follow-up would do. It’s correct, but more formal and heavier.
phrases.pronunciation: In fast speech, ‘any update on’ often sounds like EN-ee-up-DATE-on, with the strongest stress on ‘date’.

phrases.text: No rush — I just want to make sure…
phrases.meaning: This tells the other person the request is not urgent, while still explaining why you’re following up. It keeps the message considerate without making it vague.
phrases.use: Use when you genuinely do not need an immediate answer but want to prevent a task from getting forgotten or moving in the wrong direction.
phrases.avoid: Don’t say ‘No rush’ if there actually is a deadline. Mixed signals make prioritization harder.
phrases.example: No rush — I just want to make sure we’re still planning to keep the form context authoring-only before I finish the editor state changes.
phrases.mistake: Avoid over-softening with long phrases like ‘Sorry to bother you, whenever you have time, if possible…’. A simple ‘No rush’ is enough.
phrases.pronunciation: Pause slightly after ‘No rush’. Then say ‘I just wanna make sure’ naturally in speech; in writing, keep ‘want to’.

dialogue: Just checking in on the table header design. Do we have the final spacing for the mobile version?
Not yet — I should have it after today’s review.
Got it. Any update on whether Search stays visible by default?
Yes, Search stays on by default.
Perfect. No rush — I just want to make sure I’m not building the settings around an outdated version of the design.
Makes sense. I’ll send you the final spacing once it’s approved.
exercise: Write a Slack follow-up using ‘Just checking in on…’ for something you’re waiting on from product, design, or backend.
Write a short ‘Any update on…?’ message about a PR, staging deploy, API change, or decision.
Write a message using ‘No rush — I just want to make sure…’ where the answer is helpful but not urgent.
Bonus: combine two of today’s phrases into one natural two-sentence Slack message.
mixedDialogue: Just following up on the mobile breakpoint decision. I am waiting on that before I finish the canvas sizing.
I should have the final value after the design review.
Sounds good. When you get a chance, can you drop it in the thread?
No rush, but before I go too far down this path I want to make sure I am not building against an outdated breakpoint.
Makes sense. I will send the final value today.
Perfect. I will pick this back up once it is confirmed.

title: Closing the Loop
theme: Confirming the plan and moving work forward without sounding stiff
review: Spaced review: Day 14 ‘One thing to watch out for is…’ raises a risk without making it sound catastrophic; Day 15 ‘Before I go too far down this path…’ checks an assumption before investing more time; Day 16 ‘Just following up on…’ politely returns to something already discussed. Today, focus on making sure everyone leaves a discussion with the same plan.

phrases.meaning: Let me summarize what we agreed to do. Natural, practical, and slightly informal; especially useful at the end of a Slack thread, meeting, PR discussion, or product conversation because it turns a messy discussion into one clear next step.
phrases.use: Use after people have discussed options and you want to confirm the final direction before implementation.
phrases.avoid: Don’t use it before the team has actually agreed. If the decision is still open, say ‘My understanding is…’ or ‘I’d lean toward…’ instead. Also avoid using it to quietly declare your own preference as if everyone already agreed.
phrases.example: So the plan is to pass the form slug into the template editor and use it only for field lookup.
phrases.mistake: Less natural in a casual team conversation: ‘Therefore, our final implementation plan will be…’. Better: ‘So the plan is…’.
phrases.pronunciation: ‘So the’ is usually light and quick, almost ‘suh-thuh.’ Put the stress on ‘plan’ and on the important action that follows.

phrases.meaning: We have enough agreement or information, so I’m going to proceed with this action. It sounds confident and proactive without being dramatic, and is very common when closing a discussion or acknowledging a decision.
phrases.use: Use when the direction is clear and you are ready to act: updating a PR, changing a component, adding a test, or implementing a confirmed UX decision.
phrases.avoid: Don’t use it if you still need a decision or approval. In that case, ask first instead of sounding as if the decision is already made.
phrases.example: I’ll go ahead and remove the fixed-height wrapper so the page owns the scroll.
phrases.mistake: Avoid ‘I will proceed to do the changes.’ Natural: ‘I’ll go ahead and make the changes.’ After ‘go ahead and,’ use the base verb: ‘go ahead and update,’ not ‘go ahead and updating.’
phrases.pronunciation: ‘I’ll go ahead and’ often compresses in fast speech to something like ‘ahl-go-uh-head-n.’ Keep the final action verb clear and stressed.

phrases.meaning: Those steps should be enough for what we need. It closes the loop without claiming absolute certainty; ‘should’ keeps it slightly cautious, which fits engineering work where edge cases can still exist.
phrases.use: Use after listing the changes, tests, checks, or next steps that you believe fully address the task.
phrases.avoid: Don’t use it when you already know there are unresolved blockers or major unknowns. It can sound dismissive if important work is still open.
phrases.example: I’ll fix the scroll owner, add the sticky header test, and check the empty state. That should cover it.
phrases.mistake: Avoid ‘That should be enough for everything.’ It can sound too broad or overconfident. ‘That should cover it’ is more natural and refers to the current scope.
phrases.pronunciation: ‘Should cover it’ links smoothly: ‘shud-kuv-er-it.’ Stress ‘cover.’

dialogue: Did we settle the sticky table behavior?
Yep. So the plan is to keep page-level scrolling and make the header sticky against the page.
Right — no inner scroll inside the table.
Great. I’ll go ahead and remove the remaining fixed-height wrapper and update the regression test.
I’ll add one empty-state case too. That should cover it.
mixedDialogue: Just following up on the mobile editor work — are you still waiting on anything?
Before I go too far down this path, can you sanity-check one thing: the toolbar should stay fixed while the canvas scrolls, right?
Perfect. So the plan is to reuse the existing toolbar container instead of creating a mobile-only one.
One thing to watch out for is the narrow 390px state.
Good point. I’ll go ahead and add a 390px regression case. That should cover it.
exercise: Pick one task you are currently working on and summarize the agreed direction with ‘So the plan is…’.
Say exactly what you will do next using ‘I’ll go ahead and…’.
List the final checks you would make, then finish with ‘That should cover it’ only if the scope really is covered.
Bonus: write a 4-message Slack thread that starts with a Day 16 follow-up phrase and ends with one of today’s phrases.
quiz: The team has agreed on one implementation after discussing three options. Which phrase naturally summarizes the decision?
You have enough information and want to tell the team you are starting the change now. Which phrase fits best?
You listed the code change, regression test, and final check, and you believe nothing else is needed for this scope. Which phrase closes the message naturally?
habit: At the end of a technical discussion, do not leave the next step implicit. Summarize the plan, name your action, and close the loop. It makes you sound clear, dependable, and easy to work with.

title: Reproducing Bugs Clearly
theme: Describing what you can and cannot reproduce without overclaiming
review: Spaced review: Day 8 ‘From what I can tell…’ gives a current conclusion without pretending you have every detail; Day 11 ‘That explains why…’ connects a discovered cause to visible behavior; Day 14 ‘One thing to watch out for is…’ flags a risk without making it sound catastrophic. Today, focus on exactly where a bug reproduces, where it does not, and what condition seems to trigger it.

phrases.meaning: I have personally seen the same bug under this environment or condition. It sounds precise and useful because it tells the team the issue is confirmed rather than just reported.
phrases.use: Use after you have reliably triggered the bug yourself and can name the browser, device, page, environment, or state where it happens.
phrases.avoid: Don’t say it if you have not actually reproduced the issue yet. If you only saw a report, say ‘I haven’t tried to reproduce it yet’ or ‘I’ll take a look.’
phrases.example: I can reproduce this on Chrome at the 390px mobile breakpoint.
phrases.mistake: Less natural in casual team chat: ‘I succeeded to reproduce the issue.’ Natural: ‘I can reproduce it.’ or ‘I was able to reproduce it.’ ‘Replicate’ is understandable, but ‘reproduce’ is the more common engineering word for bugs.
phrases.pronunciation: ‘Reproduce’ is stressed at the end: ree-pruh-DOOS. Keep ‘I can’ light and stress ‘reproduce’ and the environment that follows.

phrases.text: I can’t seem to reproduce it.
phrases.meaning: I tried, but I’m not seeing the bug yet. The word ‘seem’ leaves room for a missing condition instead of implying the other person’s report is wrong.
phrases.use: Use after you have made a real attempt to reproduce an issue and it is not happening in your setup, browser, environment, or flow.
phrases.avoid: Don’t use it before you have actually tried. If you have not checked yet, say ‘I haven’t dug into it yet.’ Also don’t use it dismissively as if the bug cannot exist just because you cannot reproduce it.
phrases.example: I can’t seem to reproduce it in preview. Does it only happen in the published app?
phrases.mistake: Unnatural: ‘I cannot reproduce it for me.’ Natural: ‘I can’t reproduce it on my side.’ or ‘I can’t seem to reproduce it locally.’
phrases.pronunciation: ‘I can’t seem to’ often flows together like ‘I-can’t-seem-tuh.’ Stress ‘seem’ lightly and the environment you checked.

phrases.text: It only seems to happen when…
phrases.meaning: So far, I’m seeing a pattern: the bug appears under this specific condition. It helps narrow the investigation without claiming you have already proven the root cause.
phrases.use: Use when you can reproduce the issue under one condition but not others, and you want to describe the strongest pattern you have found so far.
phrases.avoid: If you have fully proven the condition, you can be more direct: ‘It happens when…’ If you have only seen the issue once, avoid presenting a one-off observation as a reliable pattern.
phrases.example: It only seems to happen when the table crosses the mobile breakpoint without a full remount.
phrases.mistake: ‘It happens only when…’ is grammatically correct, but stronger. Use ‘It only seems to happen when…’ while you are still narrowing the behavior. Avoid vague endings like ‘It happens in some situations.’ Name the condition if you know it.
phrases.pronunciation: ‘Only seems to’ flows like ‘OHN-lee-seems-tuh.’ Stress the condition after ‘when,’ because that is the useful part.

dialogue: The sticky header disappears after I resize the editor.
I can reproduce this on Chrome when I switch from desktop down to 390px.
Does it happen in the published app too?
I can’t seem to reproduce it there.
It only seems to happen when the editor crosses the breakpoint without a full remount.
mixedDialogue: I’m seeing the table header jump after switching into mobile preview.
I can reproduce this on Safari in the editor preview.
I can’t seem to reproduce it there. It only seems to happen when the layout changes breakpoint while keeping the same scroll container.
So the scroll state might be the difference?
From what I can tell, yes. That explains why a fresh mobile load is fine but resizing into mobile is not.
Anything else we should be careful about?
One thing to watch out for is forcing a remount that also wipes in-progress form state. I’d fix the scroll ownership first.
exercise: Write one real or believable bug report using ‘I can reproduce this on…’ and name the exact environment or condition.
Write a follow-up using ‘I can’t seem to reproduce it’ and ask one useful question that would help you narrow the difference.
Describe a conditional bug using ‘It only seems to happen when…’ with a concrete trigger.
Bonus: write a 5-message debugging thread that starts with reproduction status and ends with one Day 14 risk phrase.
habit: When reporting a bug, separate three things: where you confirmed it, where you did not see it, and what condition appears to trigger it. That gives teammates something they can actually test instead of just a vague ‘works for me / broken for me’ update.

title: Making Careful Commitments
theme: Giving realistic timelines and commitments without sounding vague or overpromising
review: Spaced review: Day 13 ‘I’m waiting on…’ names a dependency without automatically calling it a blocker; Day 17 ‘So the plan is…’ summarizes the agreed direction after a discussion; Day 18 ‘I can reproduce this on…’ clearly says where a bug is confirmed. Today, focus on communicating how confident you are in a timeline instead of making every estimate sound like a guarantee.

phrases.meaning: Based on what I know right now, I expect I can do this. It sounds reasonably confident, but it is not a hard guarantee. In work chat, this is useful when the task looks achievable but there is still normal uncertainty around debugging, reviews, or dependencies.
phrases.use: Use when someone asks whether you can finish, test, review, or ship something and you have a good reason to think the answer is yes.
phrases.avoid: Don’t use it for a hard promise you have already committed to, and don’t use it when a major unknown dependency could completely change the timeline. In that case, explain the dependency first.
phrases.example: I should be able to get the sticky-header fix onto staging today.
phrases.mistake: Less natural: ‘I think I can probably be able to finish it.’ Natural: ‘I should be able to finish it.’ Also, ‘should’ here usually means a realistic expectation, not weak confidence.
phrases.pronunciation: ‘I should be able to’ often becomes ‘I-shud-be-able-tuh.’ Keep ‘able’ clear and stress the action that follows.

phrases.meaning: This is my target. It gives the team a useful expectation without pretending the timing is guaranteed, and it sounds proactive because you are naming a concrete goal instead of saying ‘sometime later.’
phrases.use: Use for a target such as opening a PR, getting something to staging, finishing a test pass, or wrapping up a task by a certain point.
phrases.avoid: Don’t use it when the timing is already a firm agreed deadline; then be direct. Also don’t use it without a useful target: ‘I’m aiming to work on it’ is vague.
phrases.example: I’m aiming to have the PR ready before the afternoon review.
phrases.mistake: ‘My aim is to finish it today’ is correct but formal for normal Slack conversation. Natural: ‘I’m aiming to finish it today.’
phrases.pronunciation: ‘I’m aiming to’ flows like ‘I’m-AIM-ing-tuh.’ Stress ‘aiming’ and the time or result you are targeting.

phrases.meaning: Assuming there are no new urgent issues or unexpected blockers, this is what I expect to happen. It is a natural way to add a realistic condition without giving a long list of every possible risk.
phrases.use: Use when your estimate is reasonable, but your workday could still change because of bugs, reviews, support issues, or higher-priority work.
phrases.avoid: Don’t use it as a constant escape clause after every commitment. If there is a specific known dependency, name it directly instead of hiding it behind this phrase.
phrases.example: If nothing else comes up, I should have the PR ready today.
phrases.mistake: Less natural: ‘If no other things happen…’ Natural: ‘If nothing else comes up…’ In workplace English, ‘comes up’ means an unexpected task, issue, or situation appears.
phrases.pronunciation: ‘Nothing else comes up’ links naturally: ‘nothing-else-comes-up.’ Stress ‘else’ lightly and the final result of the sentence.

dialogue: Do you think you can get the mobile toolbar change onto staging today?
I should be able to. I’m aiming to have the PR ready by mid-afternoon.
Any risks I should know about?
Nothing major right now. If nothing else comes up, I’ll merge after the final responsive check and verify it on staging.
Perfect. Keep me posted if that changes.
mixedDialogue: Can we close the sticky-header issue today?
I should be able to. I can reproduce this on Safari now, and the remaining fix is pretty small.
I’m waiting on the staging deploy, but I can finish the frontend checks meanwhile. I’m aiming to have the PR ready before the next review.
So the plan is to merge once staging is green and then re-check Safari?
Exactly. If nothing else comes up, that should all be done today.
I’ll keep you posted if the deploy changes the plan.
exercise: Write one realistic commitment for a current task using ‘I should be able to…’.
Give one concrete target using ‘I’m aiming to…’. Include a useful result or time, not just ‘work on it.’
Write one sentence using ‘If nothing else comes up…’ for a task that could still be interrupted by other work.
Bonus: write a 5-message standup or Slack thread that includes one Day 13 dependency phrase and one of today’s phrases.
habit: When you give a timeline, communicate your confidence level as clearly as the date or target. ‘I should be able to…’ means likely, ‘I’m aiming to…’ means target, and ‘If nothing else comes up…’ explains the normal uncertainty around the plan.

title: Working Through Ambiguity
theme: Clarifying unclear product or implementation details without making the conversation heavy
review: Spaced review: Day 10 ‘My understanding is that…’ summarizes how you currently interpret a requirement; Day 15 ‘Before I go too far down this path…’ checks an assumption before investing too much time; Day 17 ‘So the plan is…’ summarizes the agreed direction once the decision is actually made. Today, focus on surfacing the unclear part, asking about intended behavior, and stating a safe working assumption.

phrases.meaning: What direction are we currently leaning toward for this part? It is collaborative and open-ended, and it does not assume there is already one correct answer. That makes it especially natural in product, design, and implementation discussions.
phrases.use: Use when a decision is still being shaped: UX behavior, scope, defaults, edge cases, naming, or implementation direction.
phrases.avoid: Don’t use it for a simple factual question with one known answer. If you only need to know whether something is enabled, ask directly. Also avoid using it when you already have a strong recommendation but pretend you are completely neutral.
phrases.example: How are we thinking about the empty state when all table controls are hidden?
phrases.mistake: Less natural in casual work chat: ‘What is our thinking regarding this matter?’ Natural: ‘How are we thinking about this?’
phrases.pronunciation: ‘How are we’ often compresses to something like ‘how-er-we.’ Stress the topic after ‘about.’

phrases.meaning: What behavior do we actually intend here? It is a practical way to turn a vague requirement into a concrete product or implementation question.
phrases.use: Use when you need to clarify behavior: whether something persists, resets, stays visible, updates live, applies everywhere, or only affects one context.
phrases.avoid: Don’t use it for something that is already a confirmed requirement. If the decision is settled, state it directly instead of reopening it accidentally.
phrases.example: Do we want this to update immediately when the form changes, or only when the editor reopens?
phrases.mistake: Less natural: ‘Do we want that this stays visible?’ Natural: ‘Do we want this to stay visible?’ After ‘want this to,’ use the base verb: stay, update, reset, persist.
phrases.pronunciation: ‘Do we want this to’ often sounds like ‘d’we-want-this-tuh.’ Keep the action verb clear because that is the important part.

phrases.text: I’m assuming … unless you had something else in mind.
phrases.meaning: I need a working interpretation so I can continue, but I’m explicitly leaving room for correction. It is more proactive than simply asking a question because it tells the team what you will do if nobody objects.
phrases.use: Use when the ambiguity is small enough that you can safely continue with a reasonable default while inviting correction.
phrases.avoid: Don’t use it for security, destructive behavior, data loss, billing, permissions, or another high-impact decision where explicit confirmation is necessary before proceeding.
phrases.example: I’m assuming the mobile canvas still uses the public-form breakpoint unless you had something else in mind.
phrases.mistake: Less natural: ‘I suppose this is the behavior if you don’t think differently.’ Natural: ‘I’m assuming this is the behavior unless you had something else in mind.’
phrases.pronunciation: ‘I’m assuming’ is stressed on SOOM: ‘I’m-uh-SOOM-ing.’ The second half is usually light: ‘unless-you-had-something-else-in-mind.’

dialogue: We need the table settings ready for the next app-editor release, but the empty state isn’t fully specified yet.
How are we thinking about the empty state when the title, Search, and New row button are all hidden?
Good question. I still want the table itself to stay visible.
Got it. Do we want this to show a small ‘No rows yet’ state, or just the empty table shell?
A small empty state would be better.
Perfect. I’m assuming it should use the existing empty-state component unless you had something else in mind.
mixedDialogue: The mobile editor should feel the same as desktop, but the field settings panel is getting crowded.
Before I go too far down this path, how are we thinking about the panel on a 390px canvas?
It probably needs to behave more like a sheet.
My understanding is that editing stays fully live. Do we want this to open over the canvas rather than shrink it?
Great. I’m assuming we reuse the existing sheet primitive unless you had something else in mind.
That’s what I had in mind.
Perfect. So the plan is to keep live editing, open settings as an overlay sheet, and leave the canvas width unchanged.
exercise: Pick one unclear product or frontend detail and ask about it using ‘How are we thinking about…?’
Turn one vague requirement into a concrete behavior question using ‘Do we want this to…?’
Write one safe working assumption using ‘I’m assuming … unless you had something else in mind.’
Bonus: write a 5-message Slack thread that starts with a Day 15 clarification phrase and ends with ‘So the plan is…’.
habit: When a requirement is unclear, don’t ask a huge vague question like ‘What should we do here?’ Narrow it down. Ask about the specific decision, describe the intended behavior you need clarified, and offer a safe working assumption when appropriate. That keeps the conversation fast without quietly inventing requirements.

title: Handling PR Feedback
theme: Responding to code-review feedback constructively without sounding defensive
review: Spaced review: Day 4 ‘Could we simplify this a bit?’ questions unnecessary complexity collaboratively; Day 7 ‘My only concern is…’ raises one important worry without rejecting the whole idea; Day 14 ‘I don’t think this is a blocker, but…’ makes review severity clear. Today, focus on acknowledging a useful catch, explaining the context behind your original choice, and deciding whether the requested change belongs in the current PR.

phrases.meaning: You noticed something useful that I missed. It is short, warm, and very natural in PR comments and Slack, and it shows appreciation without turning a small review comment into a big apology.
phrases.use: Use when a reviewer points out a real bug, overlooked edge case, typo, inconsistent state, missing test, or implementation detail you genuinely missed.
phrases.avoid: Don’t use it when you actually disagree with the feedback or when the comment is purely subjective. In that case, explain your reasoning instead of pretending they found a mistake.
phrases.example: Good catch — that branch can leave the mobile toolbar state stale.
phrases.mistake: Less natural for normal team chat: ‘Thank you for catching my mistake.’ Natural: ‘Good catch.’ Also avoid apologizing heavily for every tiny review comment; a simple acknowledgement is usually enough.
phrases.pronunciation: ‘Good catch’ is short and punchy. The final d in ‘good’ often blends into ‘catch,’ almost like ‘goo(d)-catch.’ Stress ‘catch.’

phrases.meaning: I based my decision on this existing reference, behavior, design, or assumption. It explains where your implementation came from without sounding like you are blaming someone else.
phrases.use: Use when a reviewer asks why you implemented something a certain way and there was a reasonable source behind it: an existing component, previous behavior, a design, an API response, or an earlier discussion.
phrases.avoid: Don’t use it as an excuse to avoid fixing something. If the reviewer found a real problem, explain the context and then say what you’ll change.
phrases.example: I was going off the existing published-form behavior, which keeps Search visible by default.
phrases.mistake: Less conversational: ‘I implemented it based on what I had seen before.’ Natural: ‘I was going off the existing behavior.’ Also avoid ‘I was going from…’ in this meaning; ‘going off’ is the natural phrase.
phrases.pronunciation: ‘I was going off’ flows together like ‘I-wuz-go-ing-off.’ Stress the reference that comes after it: the EXISTING behavior, the DESIGN, the API response.

phrases.text: I can fold that into this PR.
phrases.meaning: That change is related and small enough that I can include it in the current pull request. It sounds practical and gives the reviewer a clear scope decision.
phrases.use: Use when review feedback adds a closely related fix, test, cleanup, copy change, or small UX adjustment that belongs naturally with the current work.
phrases.avoid: Don’t use it when the request substantially expands scope or introduces a separate feature. In that case, say you’d rather handle it in a follow-up issue or PR.
phrases.example: Yep, the empty-state test is related. I can fold that into this PR.
phrases.mistake: More formal: ‘I can incorporate this change into the current pull request.’ Natural team English: ‘I can fold that into this PR.’ ‘Fold into’ means include something smoothly as part of a larger piece of work.
phrases.pronunciation: ‘Fold that into’ links naturally: ‘fold-that-in-tuh.’ Stress ‘fold’ and ‘PR.’

dialogue: The mobile toolbar state doesn’t reset when the form context changes.
Good catch. I was going off the existing desktop behavior, where that state survives the context switch.
For mobile I think it should reset, otherwise the sheet can reopen in the wrong state.
Yeah, that makes sense. The change is small, so I can fold that into this PR.
Could you add a regression test too?
Yep, I’ll add the state-reset case before merge.
mixedDialogue: I don’t think this is a blocker, but we’re creating a second helper just for the mobile empty state.
Good catch. I was going off the older table code, which already had separate helpers.
Could we simplify this a bit and reuse the existing empty-state mapper?
Yeah, I think that’s cleaner. I can fold that into this PR.
A small test for the hidden-header case would be useful too.
Agreed. I’ll reuse the mapper and add that test. That should cover it.
exercise: Imagine a reviewer found a real bug in your PR. Reply naturally using ‘Good catch.’
Explain one implementation choice using ‘I was going off…’ and name the existing behavior, design, API response, or component you used as reference.
Decide whether a small review request belongs in the current PR using ‘I can fold that into this PR.’
Bonus: write a 5-message PR review thread that starts with a Day 14 severity phrase and ends with one of today’s phrases.
habit: Don’t treat every PR comment like a defense of your work. Separate the three questions: Did they catch something real? What context led to your original choice? Does the requested change belong in this PR? Clear answers to those questions make review conversations faster and calmer.

title: Keeping Scope Under Control
theme: Keeping product and PR discussions focused when new requests start expanding the work
review: Spaced review: Day 9 ‘I’d keep this scoped to…’ limits a change to the part that actually belongs in the current version; Day 14 ‘I don’t think this is a blocker, but…’ makes review severity explicit; Day 21 ‘I can fold that into this PR.’ includes a small related change when it really belongs in the current PR. Today, focus on the opposite situation too: a new idea may be reasonable, but it does not necessarily belong in this release or PR.

phrases.text: Do we need this for this release?
phrases.meaning: Is this required now, or could it wait? It is direct but collaborative. You are not rejecting the idea; you are checking priority and timing before the task grows.
phrases.use: Use when a product, design, or technical request appears late in the work and you need to know whether it is actually required for the current release, milestone, or PR.
phrases.avoid: Don’t use it for something that is obviously necessary for correctness, security, data integrity, or a confirmed acceptance criterion. In those cases, the issue belongs in the release whether it is convenient or not.
phrases.example: Do we need this for this release, or can the advanced empty state come afterward?
phrases.mistake: Less conversational: ‘Is this necessary in this release?’ It is grammatically fine, but it can sound more formal and binary. Natural: ‘Do we need this for this release?’ Also avoid using the question sarcastically; the tone should genuinely ask about priority.
phrases.pronunciation: ‘Do we need this’ often compresses to something like ‘d’we-NEED-this.’ Stress ‘need’ and ‘release.’

phrases.text: Could we park that for a follow-up?
phrases.meaning: The idea may be useful, but can we deliberately move it to a later issue or PR? In workplace English, ‘park’ means temporarily set something aside without losing it.
phrases.use: Use when an idea is valid but would expand the current scope, delay the PR, or mix a separate concern into the work you are already trying to finish.
phrases.avoid: Don’t use it to postpone a real bug that affects the core requirement. Also don’t ‘park’ something without making sure it has a clear follow-up owner or issue if it genuinely matters.
phrases.example: The animation improvement makes sense. Could we park that for a follow-up and keep this PR focused on the mobile layout?
phrases.mistake: More formal: ‘Could we postpone this requirement to a subsequent task?’ Natural: ‘Could we park that for a follow-up?’ ‘Park’ is informal-professional, so it fits Slack, meetings, and PR discussion well; for external customer communication, use clearer wording such as ‘handle that in a follow-up.’
phrases.pronunciation: ‘Could we park that’ flows like ‘could-we-PARK-that.’ Stress ‘park’ and ‘follow-up.’

phrases.text: I don’t want this to snowball into…
phrases.meaning: I’m worried one small addition will keep growing into a much larger piece of work. A snowball gets larger as it rolls, so the phrase is a natural way to talk about uncontrolled scope growth.
phrases.use: Use when a small-looking request starts pulling in extra state, APIs, components, migrations, tests, or UX decisions that are outside the original goal.
phrases.avoid: Don’t use it for every extra task. It can sound resistant if the added work is genuinely small and clearly belongs in scope. Explain what expansion you are worried about so the phrase does not sound vague.
phrases.example: I’m fine adding the flag, but I don’t want this to snowball into a full permissions refactor.
phrases.mistake: Less natural: ‘I don’t want this to become bigger and bigger and bigger.’ Natural: ‘I don’t want this to snowball into…’ After ‘snowball into,’ name the larger thing you want to avoid: ‘a redesign,’ ‘a refactor,’ ‘another API,’ etc.
phrases.pronunciation: ‘Snowball into’ links smoothly: ‘SNOW-ball-in-tuh.’ Stress ‘snowball’ and the larger outcome that follows.

dialogue: While we’re updating the template editor, could we also let users connect multiple forms at once?
Do we need this for this release? The current requirement only needs one form for field lookup.
It would be useful, but it isn’t required for launch.
In that case, could we park that for a follow-up?
Sure. I don’t want to delay the current work.
Same. Multi-form support touches persistence, switching state, and piping behavior, and I don’t want this to snowball into a much bigger editor change.
mixedDialogue: I don’t think this is a blocker, but could we also clean up the old table-state helper while we’re here?
The cleanup is valid, but do we need this for this release? I’d keep this scoped to the sticky-header regression.
The helper is messy, but it isn’t causing the bug.
Then could we park that for a follow-up? I don’t want this to snowball into a table-state refactor.
Makes sense. What about adding one regression test for the hidden-header case?
That’s directly related, so I can fold that into this PR.
exercise: Think of one feature request that could reasonably wait. Ask about it using ‘Do we need this for this release?’
Take one valid but separate PR suggestion and respond with ‘Could we park that for a follow-up?’
Describe one small change that could expand badly using ‘I don’t want this to snowball into…’. Be specific about what larger work you want to avoid.
Bonus: write a 5-message PR or product thread where you keep one related change in the PR but move another idea to a follow-up.
quiz: A reviewer suggests a separate refactor that is useful but not needed to fix the current bug. Which phrase would naturally move it out of the current PR?
A PM adds a late feature idea and you are unsure whether launch depends on it. Which phrase checks the priority without rejecting the idea?
A tiny new setting now seems to require new persistence, new API behavior, and several additional UI states. Which phrase describes your concern naturally?
habit: Before accepting every new idea into an active task, separate ‘good idea’ from ‘required now.’ Keep small related fixes in scope, deliberately move separate ideas to follow-ups, and call out when a change is starting to grow beyond the original goal.

title: Choosing Between Good Options
theme: Making a clear recommendation when more than one option is reasonable
review: Spaced review: Day 6 ‘The trade-off is…’ explains what you gain and what you give up; Day 7 ‘I see where you’re coming from.’ shows you understand the other person’s reasoning before adding your own view; Day 17 ‘So the plan is…’ summarizes the decision after the discussion is settled. Today, focus on the middle: acknowledge a valid option, state a considered preference, and separate flexible details from the constraint that actually matters.

phrases.meaning: There is a reasonable argument in favor of this option. It lets you acknowledge that an alternative has real advantages even if it is not the option you ultimately prefer, so it sounds thoughtful and balanced rather than argumentative.
phrases.use: Use when comparing two valid technical, UX, or product directions and you want to recognize the benefit of one option before making a recommendation.
phrases.avoid: Don’t use it for something that is clearly incorrect, unsafe, or outside the requirement. You do not need to manufacture a balanced argument when one option simply does not work.
phrases.example: There’s a case for keeping the mobile state separate because it makes the component easier to reason about.
phrases.mistake: Less natural in everyday team chat: ‘There are arguments which support this solution.’ Natural: ‘There’s a case for this approach.’ Be careful with ‘case’: here it means a reasonable argument, not a test case or edge case.
phrases.pronunciation: ‘There’s a case for’ flows together naturally: ‘therez-uh-CASE-fer.’ Stress ‘case’ and the benefit that follows.

phrases.meaning: If I had to choose based on what we know now, I would probably choose this. It is a thoughtful preference: a little more considered than ‘I’d lean toward…’, but still open to new information.
phrases.use: Use when both options can work but you have a technical or product preference based on simplicity, consistency, maintenance, UX, or risk.
phrases.avoid: Don’t use it when the decision is already fixed by a requirement, or when you need to be very direct about a confirmed bug. It is a recommendation, not a statement of fact.
phrases.example: I’d be inclined to reuse the existing permission helper rather than add another manager-specific check.
phrases.mistake: Avoid: ‘I am more inclined for using the existing component.’ Natural: ‘I’d be inclined to use the existing component.’ After ‘inclined to,’ use the base verb: ‘to keep,’ ‘to reuse,’ ‘to split.’
phrases.pronunciation: ‘Inclined’ is pronounced ‘in-KLYND.’ In fast speech, ‘I’d be inclined to’ flows like ‘eye-d-be-in-KLYND-tuh.’ Stress ‘inclined’ and the action you prefer.

phrases.text: I’m fine either way, as long as…
phrases.meaning: I do not have a strong preference between the two options, but this condition matters. It separates flexible implementation details from the part you actually care about.
phrases.use: Use when two implementations, designs, or workflows are both acceptable and you want the team to decide freely as long as an important constraint is preserved.
phrases.avoid: Don’t say you are ‘fine either way’ when you actually have a meaningful concern. State the concern instead, otherwise you may sound agreeable now and resistant later.
phrases.example: I’m fine either way, as long as we keep one source of truth for the permission check.
phrases.mistake: Less natural: ‘For me both ways are okay if…’ Natural: ‘I’m fine either way, as long as…’ Also note that ‘either way’ normally refers to two clear alternatives already in the conversation.
phrases.pronunciation: ‘Either way’ may be ‘EE-ther way’ or ‘EYE-ther way’; both are standard. ‘As long as’ often links to ‘az-long-az.’ Stress the condition after it.

dialogue: For the mobile field settings, we can keep the current side panel or switch to the sheet component.
There’s a case for keeping the side panel because it matches desktop more closely.
True, but it gets cramped at 390px.
Yeah. Given that, I’d be inclined to use the sheet on mobile.
Would you want a separate state model for it?
I’m fine either way, as long as the selected field and unsaved changes still have one source of truth.
mixedDialogue: For project access, we can hide the action in the UI or keep it visible and let the permission check reject it.
I see where you’re coming from with keeping the UI simple. There’s a case for a backend-style guard too, because it gives us a second layer of protection.
Which direction would you take on the frontend?
I’d be inclined to hide actions the user cannot use. The trade-off is a little more permission-aware UI, but the experience is clearer.
I can work with either approach.

Same. I’m fine either way, as long as the permission helper stays the single source of truth. If we agree on hiding it, so the plan is to reuse that helper everywhere rather than duplicate role checks.
exercise: Compare two reasonable frontend approaches and write one sentence using ‘There’s a case for…’.
Pick the option you currently prefer and explain it using ‘I’d be inclined to…’.
Think of a decision where both options are acceptable. Write ‘I’m fine either way, as long as…’ and name the one condition that matters.
Bonus: write a 5-message product or PR discussion that includes ‘The trade-off is…’ plus at least two of today’s phrases.
habit: When two options are both workable, do not force false certainty. Acknowledge the valid argument, state your current preference, and make the non-negotiable constraint explicit. That makes your technical opinions sound confident without making collaboration harder.

title: Untangling Misunderstandings
theme: Correcting misunderstandings and separating related issues without sounding defensive
review: Spaced review: Day 14 “I don’t think this is a blocker, but…” helps label a concern without overstating its severity; Day 17 “So the plan is…” closes a discussion by making the agreed next step explicit; Day 21 “Good catch.” acknowledges a real issue quickly without turning it into a big apology. Today’s focus is clarifying when a thread is mixing two different questions.

phrases.text: I think we’re talking about two different things.
