phrases.meaning: We may both be making reasonable points, but we are referring to different behaviors, scopes, or problems. It is a gentle way to correct the direction of a conversation without saying “You misunderstood me.”
phrases.use: Use when a thread mixes two related but distinct topics: project access vs workspace access, rollout status vs QA status, a product decision vs a bug, or one endpoint vs another.
phrases.avoid: Don’t use it if you are definitely discussing the same exact fact and one side is simply incorrect. In that case, state the evidence directly. Also avoid saying it with a frustrated tone; the phrase works because it sounds like clarification, not accusation.
phrases.example: I think we’re talking about two different things: project access is fixed, but workspace-level redirect behavior is a separate issue.
phrases.mistake: Less natural: “We are speaking about two different subjects.” Natural: “I think we’re talking about two different things.” Another useful variant is “I think we might be mixing two things here.”
phrases.pronunciation: “We’re talking about” usually flows together: “weer-TAW-king-uh-bout.” Stress “two different things.”

phrases.text: That’s not quite what I’m seeing.
phrases.meaning: My observation is a little different from yours. It is a polite factual disagreement. “Not quite” softens the sentence, so it sounds less confrontational than “That’s wrong.”
phrases.use: Use when someone reports behavior that does not match what you see in staging, locally, in a browser, or on a specific route. It is especially useful in debugging and QA conversations.
phrases.avoid: Don’t use it for a purely subjective design preference. If someone says a layout feels crowded, discuss the UX instead of replying as if there is an objective test result.
phrases.example: That’s not quite what I’m seeing on staging. Project URLs stay on the no-access UI; the redirect only happens on the workspace root.
phrases.mistake: Unnatural: “I don’t see it like this.” Also awkward: “It is not like this from my side.” Natural: “That’s not quite what I’m seeing.” or “I’m seeing something slightly different.”
phrases.pronunciation: Stress “quite” and “seeing”: “That’s not QUITE what I’m SEE-ing.” The t in “quite” may be light in fast speech.

phrases.text: Can we separate X from Y?
phrases.meaning: Can we treat these as two distinct questions, bugs, or test paths? It is practical and collaborative. You are not saying the topics are unrelated — only that discussing or testing them separately will make the work clearer.
phrases.use: Use when one QA thread, PR, or product discussion is combining issues that can be verified or resolved independently.
phrases.avoid: Don’t split issues artificially if they share one root cause and must be fixed together. In that case, separating them may make the investigation harder.
phrases.example: Can we separate the project-permission change from the workspace redirect bug? They can be tested independently.
phrases.mistake: Less natural: “Can we divide these two subjects?” Natural: “Can we separate X from Y?” or “Can we treat these as separate issues?”
phrases.pronunciation: As a verb, “separate” is pronounced “SEP-uh-rate.” Stress the first syllable. “Can we” is usually light and quick.

dialogue: I’m still seeing a permissions issue, so I don’t think the manager-access task is ready to verify.
I think we’re talking about two different things. Which URL are you testing?
The workspace root. It redirects me home.
That’s not quite what I’m seeing on project URLs. Users without project access stay on the no-access screen there.
Right, the project URL behaves differently.
Can we separate the project-permission check from the workspace-root redirect in testing? The manager-access change can be verified independently.
mixedDialogue: I don’t think this is a blocker, but users still redirect home when the workspace request returns 403.
Good catch. That’s not quite what I’m seeing on project URLs — those stay on the no-access UI.
I was testing the workspace root, not a project route.
Ah, I think we’re talking about two different things. Can we separate the workspace-root redirect from the project no-access behavior?
Yes. The project behavior looks correct.
Great. So the plan is to keep project routes on the no-access UI and handle the workspace-root redirect as the separate case.
exercise: Think of a Slack or QA conversation where two related issues could be confused. Clarify it using “I think we’re talking about two different things.”
Disagree with an observed bug behavior politely using “That’s not quite what I’m seeing,” then add the exact environment or route you tested.
Pick two issues that can be tested independently and write a sentence using “Can we separate X from Y?”
Bonus: write a 6-message QA or PR thread that uses one Day 14 or Day 21 phrase plus at least two of today’s phrases.
habit: When a technical conversation starts feeling unnecessarily tense, check whether people are actually discussing the same thing. Clarifying the scope first is often more useful than defending your position.
